title: The Limits of Slum Maps in Identifying Heat-Vulnerable Populations: Evidence from Dhaka
content: Heat-adaptation programmes increasingly use mapped informal-settlement boundaries to decide where cooling and outreach should go, yet whether these maps reach the most heat-vulnerable residents has not been tested. We treat the slum map as a targeting instrument and evaluate it against a satellite-derived heat vulnerability index (HVI) for Dhaka, Bangladesh, built from Landsat 8/9 land surface temperature and NDVI, VIIRS night-time lights, GHSL built-up surface and WorldPop population on 1193 cells of 500 m. Using population-weighted coverage and leakage, an HVI-ranked concentration index and a nested Theil decomposition, we compare slum targeting with satellite-only, ward-level and HVI-ranked rules at a fixed budget. Slum cells were 3.6 times as likely as other cells to be very-high HVI, yet at a 32% population budget, slum targeting reached only 42.7% of the very-high-HVI population (random allocation: 32.0%), with 39.2% leakage. The slum/non-slum split explained 5.1% of HVI inequality, while 54.2% lay within wards. A two-layer “dim-hot” rule matched slum targeting without any slum delineation. Slum maps are a weak proxy for satellite-measured heat vulnerability, and fine-scale, open Earth observation offers a transferable complement for heat targeting.
